glossary.definition: A ray is an infinitely thin line showing the path along which light energy travels when wavelength goes to zero.
glossary.example: A narrow laser beam in air travels along a straight ray.

glossary.definition: Geometrical optics is the study of light propagation using rays by neglecting the tiny finite wavelength of light.
glossary.example: Tracing rays through eyeglasses or a camera lens uses geometrical optics.

glossary.definition: Diffraction is the spreading of light at the edges of a very small opening because light has a finite wavelength.
glossary.example: A hole smaller than 0.1 mm blurs the sharp shadow on a screen.

glossary.definition: The refractive index n of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum c to its speed v in that medium.
glossary.example: Glass with n = 1.5 slows light to c / 1.5.

glossary.definition: A homogeneous medium is a material whose refractive index has the same constant value at every point.
glossary.example: Calm air at uniform temperature is a homogeneous medium.

glossary.definition: Optical path length is the geometric distance light travels multiplied by the refractive index of the medium.
glossary.example: Travelling 2 cm in glass of n = 1.5 gives an optical path length of 3 cm.

glossary.definition: A stationary path is a path whose travel time does not change to first order when the path is slightly shifted.
glossary.example: At the bottom of a smooth valley, a tiny step sideways does not change height.

glossary.definition: Fermat's principle states that a light ray between two points follows a path whose optical path length is stationary.
glossary.example: Light bends at water so the total travel time stays stationary.

glossary.definition: Refraction is the bending of a light ray when it crosses the boundary between two media of different refractive indices.
glossary.example: A spoon in a glass of water looks bent at the water surface.

glossary.definition: The paraxial approximation restricts rays to small angles with the optical axis so sin θ and tan θ equal θ in radians.
glossary.example: For an angle of 0.05 rad, sin 0.05 is very close to 0.05.

glossary.definition: The center of curvature C is the center of the sphere of which a curved mirror or lens surface forms a part.
glossary.example: A normal line drawn at any point on a spherical surface passes through C.

glossary.definition: A meridional ray is a ray that stays inside a single flat plane containing the optical axis.
glossary.example: Any ray starting from a point on the optical axis is a meridional ray.

glossary.definition: A thin lens is a lens whose thickness is very small compared to the object distance, image distance, and surface radii.
glossary.example: A thin spectacle lens allows all distances to be measured from its center P.

glossary.definition: A principal focus is an axial point paired with rays parallel to the axis either after or before passing through the lens.
glossary.example: Sunlight parallel to the axis meets at the second principal focus F₂.

glossary.definition: Lateral magnification m is the ratio of the transverse image height y' to the transverse object height y.
glossary.example: If a 1 cm object forms an inverted 2 cm image, the lateral magnification is -2.

glossary.definition: The superposition principle states that when two or more waves overlap at a point, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.
glossary.example: Two crests of amplitude a₁ and a₂ meeting in phase add to form a crest of amplitude a₁ + a₂.

glossary.definition: Constructive interference occurs when two waves meet in phase so their amplitudes add; destructive interference occurs when they meet out of phase by π so their amplitudes subtract.
glossary.example: At phase difference 0, amplitude is a₁ + a₂; at phase difference π, amplitude is |a₁ - a₂|.

glossary.definition: Division of wavefront is a method of getting two coherent light beams by splitting a single wavefront at two closely spaced holes, slits, or mirrors.
glossary.example: Young's double-hole experiment splits one spherical wavefront from pinhole S at two pinholes S₁ and S₂.

glossary.definition: A nodal line is a hyperbolic curve along which waves from two coherent sources arrive out of phase by (n + ½)λ and produce minimum intensity.
glossary.example: In a ripple tank, water stays calm along the hyperbolic nodal lines between two vibrating needles.

glossary.definition: Coherent sources are wave sources whose phase difference remains constant over time, so they produce a stationary interference pattern.
glossary.example: Two slits lit by one pinhole are coherent, whereas two independent sodium lamps are incoherent.

glossary.definition: Fringe width β is the distance between two consecutive bright fringes or two consecutive dark fringes on the screen.
glossary.example: In Young's double-hole experiment, fringe width is β = λD/d.

glossary.definition: Fresnel's two-mirror arrangement uses two plane mirrors touching at a small angle θ to reflect light from a slit S into two coherent virtual sources S₁ and S₂.
glossary.example: If slit S is at distance R from mirror junction M, the virtual sources are separated by d = 2Rθ.

glossary.definition: Fresnel's biprism is a thin double prism with very small acute base angles α (~20') that refracts light from one slit into two coherent virtual images.
glossary.example: With slit S at distance a from a biprism of index n, the virtual slits are separated by d = 2a(n - 1)α.

glossary.definition: White-light interference gives a sharp white central fringe at zero path difference with a few colored fringes on either side before fading to uniform white.
glossary.example: White light helps locate the central zero-order fringe when a thin mica sheet shifts the pattern.

glossary.definition: Lloyd's mirror produces interference between waves coming directly from a slit S₁ and waves reflected at grazing incidence from a plane mirror.
glossary.example: The central fringe at the mirror edge is dark because reflection at a denser medium shifts phase by π.

glossary.definition: Stokes' relations connect the amplitude reflection and transmission coefficients across an interface by time-reversal symmetry: r₂ = -r₁ and t₁t₂ = 1 - r₁².
glossary.example: Because r₂ = -r₁, reflection at a denser medium shifts phase by π while reflection at a rarer medium has zero phase shift.

glossary.definition: Division of amplitude splits a single wave by partial reflection and transmission at two surfaces so the reflected or transmitted beams interfere.
glossary.example: A thin film in air reflects light from its upper and lower surfaces with path difference 2n₂d cos θ'.

glossary.definition: A non-reflecting film is a quarter-wave coating of thickness λ/(4n_f) and index n_f = √(n_a n_g) on glass whose two reflected waves cancel by destructive interference.
glossary.example: Coating a crown-glass lens with MgF₂ (n_f = 1.38) cuts reflection from 4% to about 1.3%.

glossary.definition: Fringes of equal thickness are interference bands seen in a thin film of varying thickness, where each fringe marks a line of constant film thickness.
glossary.example: Colored bands on a soap bubble or air wedge follow contours of constant thickness.

glossary.definition: Newton's rings are concentric circular bright and dark fringes formed in the thin air film between a convex lens surface and a plane glass plate.
glossary.example: In reflected monochromatic light, the central spot is dark and the m-th dark ring has radius √(mλR).

glossary.definition: The Michelson interferometer splits a light beam at a 45° beam splitter toward two perpendicular mirrors M₁ and M₂ and recombines the reflected beams to form fringes.
glossary.example: If N circular fringes collapse as mirror M₁ moves by d₀, the wavelength is λ = 2d₀/N.

cards.title: When light behaves like thin straight pencils
cards.meaning: Geometrical optics is the model of light as thin directional lines called rays when openings are much larger than the wavelength.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="32,90 215,34 215,146" class="s"/><line x1="115" y1="16" x2="115" y2="58" class="lk"/><line x1="115" y1="122" x2="115" y2="164" class="lk"/><line x1="215" y1="16" x2="215" y2="164" class="lk"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="34" class="lk"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="146" class="lk"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="90" class="ik"/><path d="M 62 81 A 32 32 0 0 1 62 99" class="lk"/><circle cx="32" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><text x="18" y="94" class="t">P</text><text x="115" y="13" text-anchor="middle" class="t">A</text><text x="115" y="174" text-anchor="middle" class="t">B</text><text x="162" y="82" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ray (λ→0)</text><text x="226" y="28" class="t">S</text><text x="226" y="158" class="t">S'</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the sharp cone of rays from P through wide opening AB onto screen SS'.
cards.example: Visible light has a tiny wavelength near 0.0005 cm, so ordinary lenses and mirrors are huge compared to it.
cards.bridge: In the mathematical limit where wavelength λ goes to zero, diffraction disappears and light energy follows thin paths called rays.

cards.label: 01 · §3.1 Definition
cards.title: What is geometrical optics?
cards.body: Geometrical optics treats light propagation using thin rays by neglecting the finite wavelength of light when apertures are large.

cards.title: Why denser media count as longer paths
cards.meaning: Optical path length is the vacuum distance that light would travel in the same time it takes to cross a medium.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="65" y="24" width="80" height="52" class="s ok"/><line x1="24" y1="50" x2="185" y2="50" class="lk"/><line x1="65" y1="84" x2="65" y2="142" class="gk"/><line x1="145" y1="84" x2="145" y2="112" class="gk"/><line x1="65" y1="130" x2="185" y2="130" class="ik"/><circle cx="65" cy="130" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="185" cy="130" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="105" y="42" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Glass (n = 1.5)</text><text x="105" y="68" text-anchor="middle" class="t">d = 2 cm</text><text x="125" y="118" text-anchor="middle" class="t">L_op = n d = 3 cm</text><text x="125" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Same travel time τ in vacuum</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare the 2 cm glass block (top) with the 3 cm vacuum path (bottom) that takes the exact same time.
cards.example: In glass with refractive index n = 1.5, a physical thickness of 2 cm has an optical path length of 1.5 × 2 cm = 3 cm.
cards.bridge: Because speed in a medium is c / n, the time for step ds is (n ds) / c, so integrating n ds gives the optical path length.

cards.label: 02 · §3.1 Definition
cards.title: What is optical path length?
cards.body: Optical path length is the integral of refractive index n along the geometric path, equal to c times the travel time.

cards.title: How light chooses its path
cards.meaning: Fermat's principle says light travels along a path whose travel time is stationary compared with slightly different nearby paths.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M 30 138 Q 115 32 230 42" class="gk"/><path d="M 30 138 Q 148 148 230 42" class="gk"/><path d="M 30 138 Q 130 92 230 42" class="lk"/><path d="M 56 116 A 34 34 0 0 1 63 134" class="lk"/><circle cx="30" cy="138" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="230" cy="42" r="4" class="f"/><text x="16" y="146" class="t">A</text><text x="236" y="46" class="t">B</text><text x="82" y="52" class="t">Trial path C'</text><text x="112" y="88" class="t">Actual ray C</text><text x="148" y="148" class="t">δ ∫ n ds = 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the solid ray ACB between the two dashed trial paths where small shifts do not change travel time.
cards.example: In uniform air, the straight line between A and B has the shortest optical path. Inside an elliptical mirror, every path from focus S₁ to focus S₂ has the exact same length.
cards.bridge: Therefore the modern statement replaces 'least time' with 'stationary optical path length': δ ∫ n ds = 0, allowing a minimum, maximum, or constant value.

cards.label: 03 · §3.1 Definition
cards.title: What is Fermat's principle?
cards.body: Fermat's principle states that the actual ray path between two points makes the optical path length stationary with respect to small path variations.

cards.label: 04 · §3.2 Reflection
cards.title: Laws of reflection from Fermat's principle
cards.body: Reflecting A across mirror MN to A' makes AP + PB = A'P + PB. A straight line A'PB minimizes length, so angle i equals angle r in one plane.

cards.label: 05 · §3.2 Derivation
cards.title: Laws of refraction from Fermat's principle
cards.legend: Interface \(PQ\) separates media \(n_1, n_2\) with perpendiculars \(AM = h_1\), \(BN = h_2\), \(MR = x\), and \(RN = L - x\) (Fig. 3.5).

phases.name: Optical path
phases.why: sum optical paths n₁ AR and n₂ RB

phases.name: First medium
phases.why: write AR from right triangle AMR

phases.name: Second medium
phases.why: write RB from right triangle RBN

phases.name: Stationary path
phases.why: differentiate L_op with respect to x and set to zero

phases.name: Incidence angle
phases.why: substitute sin θ₁ in medium n₁

phases.name: Refraction angle
phases.why: substitute sin θ₂ in medium n₂ to reach Snell's law

steps.note: Write total optical path length from \(A\) to \(B\) via point \(R\) on \(PQ\).
In right triangle \(AMR\), replace \(AR\) with \(\sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\).
In right triangle \(RBN\), replace \(RB\) with \(\sqrt{(L - x)^2 + h_2^2}\) (Eq. 3.4).
Differentiate \(L_{op}\) with respect to \(x\); the chain rule on \((L - x)^2\) gives a minus sign.

ask.q: How do we find the stationary ray path as \(x\) varies?
ask.why: Fermat's principle requires differentiating the optical path with respect to \(x\).

steps.note: Set \(dL_{op}/dx = 0\) for an extremum optical path (Eq. 3.5).

ask.q: What value must \(dL_{op}/dx\) take on the actual ray path?
ask.why: At a stationary point of the optical path, the first derivative vanishes.

steps.note: In right triangle \(AMR\), substitute \(\sin\theta_1 = x/\sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\).

ask.q: What does \(x / \sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\) equal in triangle \(AMR\)?
ask.why: Side \(MR = x\) is opposite \(\theta_1\) and \(AR = \sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\) is the hypotenuse.

steps.note: In right triangle \(RBN\), substitute \(\sin\theta_2 = (L - x)/\sqrt{(L - x)^2 + h_2^2}\).
Add \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) to both sides.

ask.q: Which move places the two refraction terms on opposite sides?
ask.why: Adding \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) isolates \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) on the left and \(n_1\sin\theta_1\) on the right.

steps.note: Swap sides to obtain Snell's law of refraction (Eq. 3.6).

cards.label: 06 · §3.2 Examples
cards.title: Paraboloidal and elliptical reflectors (Examples 3.1–3.2)
cards.body: A paraboloid reflects parallel rays to its focus \(S\) (radio telescopes). An elliptical reflector sends every ray from focus \(S_1\) to focus \(S_2\) with stationary (constant) travel time (ruby laser).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When does geometrical optics accurately describe light propagation?
options: When wavelength is much smaller than apertures
When apertures are smaller than wavelength
Only when refractive index is zero
cards.why: Neglecting wavelength works when openings are much larger than the wavelength of light.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: According to the modern Fermat's principle, the optical path of a ray is:
cards.why: The ray path makes the optical path length stationary: a minimum, maximum, or constant.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In a homogeneous medium, light rays travel along ______ lines.
cards.why: With constant refractive index, a straight line minimizes the optical path between two points.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Find the optical path length for \(4\text{ cm}\) in glass of \(n = 1.5\).
cards.why: Optical path length equals \(n \times d = 1.5 \times 4\text{ cm} = 6\text{ cm}\).

sheets.title: Single spherical surface
sheets.source: Unit 2 · Ghatak §§4.2–4.3 (PDF pp. 80–82). Note: Section 4.1 is missing from the unit files and is not included.

cards.title: Why only rays close to the axis focus sharply
cards.meaning: The paraxial approximation keeps only rays that make very small angles with the symmetry axis of a curved surface.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="16" y1="105" x2="244" y2="105" class="lk"/><path d="M 132 24 Q 104 105 132 162" class="lk"/><line x1="118" y1="56" x2="118" y2="105" class="gk"/><polyline points="28,105 118,56 226,105" class="lk"/><path d="M 56 90 A 32 32 0 0 1 60 105" class="lk"/><path d="M 196 105 A 30 30 0 0 1 199 92" class="lk"/><circle cx="28" cy="105" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="118" cy="56" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="226" cy="105" r="4" class="f"/><text x="28" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="t">O</text><text x="66" y="98" class="t">α₁</text><text x="126" y="84" class="t">h</text><text x="118" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P</text><text x="226" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I</text><text x="130" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Small α₁: sin α₁ ≈ tan α₁ ≈ h/x</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the small angle arc α₁ near O where height h divided by distance x gives the angle in radians.
cards.example: At an angle of 0.1 rad (about 5.7°), sin(0.1) = 0.0998 and tan(0.1) = 0.1003, so sin φ₁ ≈ tan φ₁ ≈ φ₁.
cards.bridge: Under this small-angle rule, all paraxial rays from object point O take equal time and meet at a single image point I.

cards.label: 01 · §4.2 Definition
cards.title: What is the paraxial approximation?
cards.body: The paraxial approximation assumes rays make very small angles with the optical axis so sine and tangent equal the angle in radians.

cards.label: 02 · §4.2.1 Sign convention
cards.title: The Sign Convention at pole P
cards.body: Rays are incident from the left. With pole P as origin, distances to the right are positive, to the left are negative, and upward heights are positive.

cards.label: 03 · §4.2.2 Derivation
cards.title: The Gaussian formula for a single spherical surface
cards.legend: Spherical surface \(SPM\) separating \(n_1, n_2\) with object \(O\) at \(x = -u\), image \(I\) at \(y = v\), center \(C\) at \(r = R\), height \(h\) (Fig. 4.1(a)).

phases.name: Snell's law
phases.why: start from Snell's law and apply the paraxial approximation

phases.name: Incident angle
phases.why: express φ₁ from exterior angle of triangle OSC

phases.name: Refracted angle
phases.why: express φ₂ from exterior angle of triangle ISC

phases.name: Cancel height
phases.why: divide by h and collect distance terms

phases.name: Sign convention
phases.why: apply u = -x, v = y, and R = r

steps.note: Start from Snell's law at point \(S\) on spherical surface \(SPM\) (Eq. 4.1).
Use the paraxial approximation \(\sin\phi \approx \phi\) for small angles in radians.

ask.q: Why can \(\sin\phi_1\) and \(\sin\phi_2\) be replaced by \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\)?
options: The surface is a plane mirror
ask.why: In the paraxial approximation, all angles in radians are small so \(\sin\phi \approx \phi\).

steps.note: In triangle \(OSC\), exterior angle \(\phi_1\) equals \(\beta + \alpha_1\).

ask.q: In triangle \(OSC\), what does exterior angle \(\phi_1\) equal?
ask.why: Angle \(\phi_1\) is exterior to interior angles \(\alpha_1\) at \(O\) and \(\beta\) at \(C\).

steps.note: Substitute \(\beta \approx \tan\beta = h/r\) and \(\alpha_1 \approx \tan\alpha_1 = h/x\) (Eq. 4.2).
In triangle \(ISC\), exterior angle \(\beta = \phi_2 + \alpha_2\), so \(\phi_2 = \beta - \alpha_2\).
Substitute \(\beta \approx h/r\) and \(\alpha_2 \approx \tan\alpha_2 = h/y\) (Eq. 4.3).
Divide both sides by \(h\) so the ray height cancels out.

ask.q: Why does dividing by \(h\) show all paraxial rays focus together?
options: The equation no longer depends on \(h\)
ask.why: Once \(h\) cancels, every paraxial ray gives the same image distance \(y\).

steps.note: Collect \(x, y\) terms on the left and \(r\) terms on the right (Eq. 4.4).
Apply the sign convention \(u = -x, v = y, R = r\) to get the Gaussian formula (Eq. 4.5).

ask.q: Since object \(O\) lies left of pole \(P\), what replaces \(x\)?
ask.why: Distances to the left of \(P\) are negative, so \(u = -x\) and \(x = -u\).

cards.title: Rays that stay in one flat slice versus skew rays
cards.meaning: Meridional rays stay inside the plane that contains the optical axis, whereas skew rays twist out of a single plane.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="24,118 76,34 236,34 184,118" class="s ok"/><line x1="34" y1="76" x2="226" y2="76" class="lk"/><polyline points="52,76 128,48 204,76" class="ik"/><polyline points="64,108 134,58 196,144" class="gk"/><circle cx="52" cy="76" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="76" r="4" class="f"/><text x="46" y="94" class="t">C₁</text><text x="206" y="94" class="t">C₂</text><text x="134" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Meridional ray (in plane)</text><text x="148" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Skew ray (leaves plane)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the solid meridional ray inside the flat axial slice, while the dashed skew ray leaves the slice in 3D.
cards.example: Every ray starting from an object point on the optical axis is automatically a meridional ray.
cards.bridge: When a system has two spherical surfaces, the line joining their centers C₁ and C₂ defines the optical axis.

cards.label: 04 · §4.2.2 Definition
cards.title: What is a meridional ray?
cards.body: A meridional ray is a light ray confined to a single plane containing the optical axis, unlike a non-planar skew ray.

cards.label: 05 · §4.3 Derivation
cards.title: Reflection by a single spherical surface
cards.legend: Spherical mirror \(SPM\) with object \(O\), center \(C\), and image \(I\) to the left of pole \(P\) (\(u = -x, v = -y, R = -r\), Fig. 4.3).

phases.name: Reflection law
phases.why: equate angles of incidence and reflection at S

phases.name: Incident ray
phases.why: write φ₁ from triangle OSC and paraxial ratios

phases.name: Reflected ray
phases.why: write φ₂ from triangle CSI and paraxial ratios

phases.name: Cancel height
phases.why: divide by h and collect 1/x + 1/y

phases.name: Sign convention
phases.why: substitute u = -x, v = -y, R = -r

steps.note: At point \(S\), the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
In triangle \(OSC\), exterior angle \(\beta = \alpha_1 + \phi_1\), so \(\phi_1 = \beta - \alpha_1\).

ask.q: In triangle \(OSC\), how is \(\phi_1\) related to \(\beta\) and \(\alpha_1\)?
ask.why: Exterior angle \(\beta\) equals \(\alpha_1 + \phi_1\), so \(\phi_1 = \beta - \alpha_1\).

steps.note: Replace small angles \(\beta\) and \(\alpha_1\) by \(h/r\) and \(h/x\).
In triangle \(CSI\), exterior angle \(\alpha_2 = \beta + \phi_2\), so \(\phi_2 = \alpha_2 - \beta\).
Replace small angles \(\alpha_2\) and \(\beta\) by \(h/y\) and \(h/r\).

ask.q: What replaces \(\alpha_2\) in the paraxial approximation?
ask.why: Reflected ray \(SI\) meets the axis at distance \(y\), so \(\alpha_2 \approx h / y\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(h\).

ask.q: What is the next step to eliminate the ray height \(h\)?
ask.why: Every term has \(h\) in the numerator, so dividing by \(h\) removes it.

steps.note: Collect \(1/x + 1/y\) on the left and \(2/r\) on the right (Eq. 4.6).
Since \(O, I, C\) lie to the left of \(P\), substitute \(x = -u, y = -v, r = -R\).
Negate both sides to obtain the mirror equation (Eq. 4.7).

ask.q: Which substitution in the refraction formula also gives the mirror equation?
ask.why: Setting \(n_2 = -n_1\) in Eq. (4.5) turns Snell's law into reflection and yields Eq. (4.7).

cards.label: 06 · §4.2.2 Example
cards.title: Worked example: refraction at spherical surfaces (Example 4.1)
cards.body: First surface \(S_1 P_1 M_1\) (\(R_1 = +15\text{ cm}\)) forms image \(O'\) at \(+180\text{ cm}\). Separated by \(30\text{ cm}\), second surface \(S_2 P_2 M_2\) (\(u = +150\text{ cm}, R_2 = -25\text{ cm}\)) forms a real image at \(+33\tfrac{1}{3}\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In the Cartesian sign convention, when is object distance \(u\) positive?
options: When incident rays converge right of P
When a real object sits left of P
cards.why: Distances to the right of pole \(P\) are positive, which happens for a virtual object.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Off-axis rays that do not stay in a single plane are called ______ rays.
cards.why: Rays confined to the axial plane are meridional rays; non-planar rays are skew rays.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For a concave mirror with \(R = -60\text{ cm}\) and \(u = -80\text{ cm}\), find \(v\).

cards.title: Two spherical surfaces pressed close together
cards.meaning: A thin lens is a transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces whose thickness is negligible compared to all other distances.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="12" y1="96" x2="248" y2="96" class="lk"/><path d="M 118 26 Q 104 96 118 164 Q 132 96 118 26 Z" class="s ok"/><polyline points="26,96 118,46 218,96" class="lk"/><path d="M 50 83 A 28 28 0 0 1 54 96" class="lk"/><path d="M 192 96 A 26 26 0 0 1 195 84" class="lk"/><circle cx="26" cy="96" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="118" cy="96" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="218" cy="96" r="4" class="f"/><text x="26" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">O</text><text x="118" y="18" text-anchor="middle" class="t">t ≪ |u|, |v|</text><text x="110" y="114" text-anchor="end" class="t">P</text><text x="218" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I</text><text x="72" y="138" text-anchor="middle" class="t">u (from P)</text><text x="168" y="138" text-anchor="middle" class="t">v (from P)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the thin lens at P: thickness t is so small that both u and v are measured from P.
cards.example: Because thickness t is tiny, we measure object distance u and image distance v from one shared center P.
cards.bridge: The first surface forms an intermediate image Q at v', which immediately acts as the object for the second surface to form final image I at v.

cards.label: 01 · §4.4 Definition
cards.title: What is a thin spherical lens?
cards.body: A thin spherical lens is a medium bounded by two spherical refracting surfaces whose thickness t is very small compared to object, image, and curvature distances.

cards.label: 02 · §4.4 Derivation
cards.title: The thin lens and Lensmaker's formula
cards.legend: Lens of index \(n_2\) in medium \(n_1\) with radii \(R_1, R_2\), intermediate image \(Q\) at \(v'\), final image \(I\) at \(v\), and \(n = n_2 / n_1\) (Fig. 4.5).

phases.name: First surface
phases.why: refraction at R₁ from n₁ into n₂ forms image Q at v'

phases.name: Second surface
phases.why: refraction at R₂ from n₂ into n₁ takes Q at v' to I at v

phases.name: Combine surfaces
phases.why: add the two surface equations to eliminate v'

phases.name: Relative index
phases.why: divide by n₁ and define n = n₂ / n₁

phases.name: Focal length
phases.why: define focal length f by Lensmaker's formula

steps.note: First surface \(R_1\) refracts light from \(n_1\) into \(n_2\), forming \(Q\) at \(v'\) (Eq. 4.8).
Point \(Q\) at \(v'\) acts as object for second surface \(R_2\) from \(n_2\) into \(n_1\) (Eq. 4.9).

ask.q: For the second surface \(R_2\), what acts as its object distance?
ask.why: The image \(Q\) formed by the first surface at \(v'\) serves as the object for the second surface.

steps.note: Add Eqs. (4.8) and (4.9) so \(+n_2/v'\) and \(-n_2/v'\) cancel out.

ask.q: Why do we add Eqs. (4.8) and (4.9) together?
ask.why: Adding \(+n_2/v'\) and \(-n_2/v'\) eliminates the intermediate image position \(v'\).

steps.note: Factor \((n_2 - n_1)\) on the right, flipping the sign on \(1/R_2\).

ask.q: When \((n_2 - n_1)\) is factored out of \((n_1 - n_2)/R_2\), what remains?
ask.why: Since \(n_1 - n_2 = -(n_2 - n_1)\), factoring out \((n_2 - n_1)\) leaves \(-1/R_2\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by surrounding refractive index \(n_1\).
Write \(n = n_2 / n_1\) to obtain the thin lens formula (Eq. 4.10).
Define focal length \(f\) by Eq. (4.12) to get Eq. (4.11).

ask.q: When \(u = -\infty\) (incident parallel rays), what does \(v\) equal?
ask.why: Setting \(1/u = 0\) in \(1/v - 1/u = 1/f\) gives \(v = f\).

cards.label: 03 · §4.4 Surrounding medium
cards.title: Converging and diverging lenses in different media
cards.body: For a biconvex lens (R₁ > 0, R₂ < 0), (1/R₁ - 1/R₂) is positive. It converges light when n₂ > n₁, but diverges light when placed in a medium with n₁ > n₂ (Fig. 4.7).

cards.title: The two special focal points of any lens
cards.meaning: The first principal focus F₁ turns rays from a point into parallel rays, while the second principal focus F₂ collects incoming parallel rays to a point.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="12" y1="90" x2="248" y2="90" class="lk"/><path d="M 130 20 Q 116 90 130 160 Q 144 90 130 20 Z" class="s ok"/><polyline points="56,90 130,136 238,136" class="lk"/><polyline points="22,44 130,44 204,90" class="ik"/><circle cx="56" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="130" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><text x="56" y="78" text-anchor="middle" class="t">F₁</text><text x="122" y="106" text-anchor="end" class="t">P</text><text x="204" y="108" text-anchor="middle" class="t">F₂</text><text x="80" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ray 2 (parallel → F₂)</text><text x="184" y="154" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ray 1 (F₁ → parallel)</text><text x="92" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="t">f₁ < 0</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" class="t">f₂ > 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Ray 1 from F₁ emerging parallel, and parallel Ray 2 meeting the axis at F₂.
cards.example: For a converging lens of focal length 20 cm in air, F₁ sits at f₁ = -20 cm (left) and F₂ sits at f₂ = +20 cm (right).
cards.bridge: Setting v = ∞ gives u = f₁ (first focal length), and setting u = -∞ gives v = f₂ (second focal length).

cards.label: 04 · §4.5 Definition
cards.title: What are the first and second principal foci?
cards.body: The first principal focus F₁ is the axial object point whose refracted rays emerge parallel (v = ∞), and the second principal focus F₂ is the axial image point for incident parallel rays (u = -∞).

cards.label: 05 · §4.5 Ray tracing
cards.title: Three principal rays for graphical construction
cards.body: Ray 1 through F₁ emerges parallel to the axis. Ray 2 parallel to the axis passes through F₂. Ray 3 through lens center P passes undeviated (Fig. 4.8).

cards.label: 06 · §4.5 Different media
cards.title: Thin lens with different media on its two sides (Eqs. 4.14–4.16)
cards.body: When medium \(n_1\) is on the left and \(n_3\) on the right, setting \(v = \infty\) (Eq. 4.15) and \(u = -\infty\) (Eq. 4.16) gives \(f_2 / f_1 = -n_3 / n_1\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For a converging lens in air, what are the signs of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\)?
cards.why: For a converging lens, \(F_1\) lies on the left (\(f_1 < 0\)) and \(F_2\) lies on the right (\(f_2 > 0\)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How does a glass biconvex lens behave inside a liquid of higher refractive index?
cards.why: When \(n_2 < n_1\), \((n - 1)\) becomes negative, so \(f < 0\) and the biconvex lens diverges light.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: A paraxial ray passing through the center \(P\) of a thin lens travels ______.
cards.why: At \(u = 0\), the thin lens formula gives \(v = 0\), so the ray through \(P\) passes undeviated.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Find \(f\) in air for \(n = 1.5\), \(R_1 = +20\text{ cm}\), and \(R_2 = -20\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: 01 · §4.6 Focal distances
cards.title: Measuring object and image from the two foci
cards.body: Newton's method measures object distance x₁ from F₁ (positive if right of F₁) and image distance x₂ from F₂ (positive if right of F₂), as in Fig. 4.8.

cards.label: 02 · §4.6 Derivation
cards.title: The Newton formula
cards.legend: Object height \(y\) at \(x_1\) from \(F_1\), image height \(y'\) at \(x_2\) from \(F_2\), focal lengths \(f_1, f_2\) (Fig. 4.8(a)).

phases.name: First focus
phases.why: use similar triangles AOF₁ and LPF₁ at F₁

phases.name: Second focus
phases.why: use similar triangles KPF₂ and BIF₂ at F₂

phases.name: Equate ratios
phases.why: equate the two height ratios and cross-multiply

phases.name: Same medium
phases.why: set f₁ = -f and f₂ = f for the same surrounding medium

steps.note: Similar right triangles \(AOF_1\) and \(LPF_1\) share the angle at \(F_1\) (Eq. 4.17).
Cancel the minus signs in the numerator and denominator on the right.

move.label: Use similar triangles KPF₂ and BIF₂ (Eq. 4.18)

steps.note: In similar triangles \(KPF_2\) and \(BIF_2\) around \(F_2\), \(-y'/y = x_2/f_2\) (Eq. 4.18).

ask.q: In triangles \(KPF_2\) and \(BIF_2\), what does \(-y' / y\) equal?
ask.why: Since \(KP = y\) and \(BI = -y'\), the ratio of heights equals \(x_2 / f_2\).

steps.note: Equate the two expressions for \(-y'/y\) from Eqs. (4.17) and (4.18).
Multiply both sides by \(x_1 f_2\) to get the Newtonian lens formula (Eq. 4.19).

ask.q: Which move clears both denominators in \(f_1/x_1 = x_2/f_2\)?
ask.why: Multiplying by \(x_1 f_2\) gives \(f_1 f_2 = x_1 x_2\).

steps.note: When both sides have the same medium, Eq. (4.13) gives \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = f\).

ask.q: When the same medium surrounds the lens, what is \(f_1 f_2\)?
ask.why: Because \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = +f\), their product is \(-f^2\).

steps.note: Thus \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) must always have opposite signs (Eq. 4.20).

ask.q: Since \(x_1 x_2 = -f^2 < 0\), what must be true of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)?
ask.why: A negative product \(-f^2\) means one lies left of its focus and the other lies right.

cards.title: How tall and which way up the image is
cards.meaning: Lateral magnification compares the height of the image to the height of the object, including a sign for orientation.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="14" y1="90" x2="246" y2="90" class="lk"/><path d="M 120 22 Q 108 90 120 158 Q 132 90 120 22 Z" class="s ok"/><line x1="38" y1="90" x2="38" y2="38" class="ik"/><line x1="216" y1="90" x2="216" y2="148" class="ik"/><line x1="38" y1="38" x2="216" y2="148" class="lk"/><path d="M 96 75 A 28 28 0 0 0 92 90" class="lk"/><path d="M 148 90 A 28 28 0 0 1 144 105" class="lk"/><circle cx="120" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><text x="24" y="66" class="t">y</text><text x="38" y="106" text-anchor="middle" class="t">O</text><text x="82" y="84" class="t">θ</text><text x="152" y="104" class="t">θ</text><text x="112" y="108" text-anchor="end" class="t">P</text><text x="216" y="82" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I</text><text x="228" y="130" class="t">y'</text><text x="78" y="136" text-anchor="middle" class="t">u < 0</text><text x="170" y="60" text-anchor="middle" class="t">v > 0 (m = v/u)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the equal angle arcs θ at lens center P: similar right triangles give m = y'/y = v/u.
cards.example: A positive magnification (m > 0) means an erect image; a negative magnification (m < 0) means an inverted image.
cards.bridge: For a thin lens in one medium, similar triangles through pole P give m = y' / y = v / u = -f₁ / x₁ = -x₂ / f₂.

cards.label: 03 · §4.7 Definition
cards.title: What is lateral magnification?
cards.body: Lateral magnification m is the ratio of image height y' to object height y, where positive m means erect and negative m means inverted (Eq. 4.21).

cards.label: 04 · §4.7 Derivation
cards.title: Lateral magnification of spherical surface and thin lens
cards.legend: Object \(OA = y\) at \(u\), center of curvature \(C\) at \(R\), image \(IB = -y'\) at \(v\) (Fig. 4.9, Eqs. 4.22–4.24).

phases.name: Triangles at C
phases.why: use similar triangles AOC and ICB through center C

phases.name: Surface law
phases.why: substitute v/R and u/R from the Gaussian surface equation

phases.name: First lens surface
phases.why: write magnification m₁ for the first surface of a thin lens

phases.name: Second lens surface
phases.why: write magnification m₂ for the second surface of a thin lens

phases.name: Total magnification
phases.why: multiply m₁ and m₂ to get m = v/u

steps.note: Ray \(ACB\) along the normal at \(C\) passes undeviated, giving similar triangles \(AOC\) and \(ICB\) (Eq. 4.22).

move.label: Divide numerator and denominator by R

steps.note: Divide numerator and denominator on the right-hand side by \(R\) (Eq. 4.22).

ask.q: Why does the ray from \(A\) through \(C\) pass straight without bending?
options: It hits the spherical surface along the normal
ask.why: Any line through center of curvature \(C\) is normal to the sphere, so \(\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 0\).

steps.note: Substitute \(v/R - 1\) and \(-u/R + 1\) from Eq. (4.5).
Negate both sides and set \(m = y'/y\) for a single refracting surface (Eq. 4.23).

ask.q: What is the lateral magnification of a single surface from \(n_1\) to \(n_2\)?
ask.why: Refraction from \(n_1\) into \(n_2\) gives \(m = (n_1 v)/(n_2 u)\) (Eq. 4.23).

steps.note: For the first surface of a thin lens (\(n_1 \to n_2\)), intermediate image at \(v'\) has magnification \(m_1\).
For the second surface (\(n_2 \to n_1\)), object at \(v'\) forms image at \(v\) with magnification \(m_2\).

ask.q: How is total magnification \(m\) found for two surfaces in succession?
ask.why: The first image height is scaled again by \(m_2\), so total magnification is \(m_1 m_2\).

steps.tex: m_1 m_2 = \frac{n_1 v'}{n_2 u}\cdot\frac{n_2 v}{n_1 v'}
steps.note: Multiply the two surface magnifications \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) together.
Cancel \(n_1, n_2\) and \(v'\) to get \(m = m_1 m_2 = v/u\) (Eq. 4.24).

ask.q: Which factors cancel when \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are multiplied?
ask.why: Factors \(n_1, n_2\) and intermediate image distance \(v'\) cancel, leaving \(m = v/u\).

cards.label: 05 · §4.7 Example
cards.title: Two thin lenses separated by 8 cm (Example 4.3)
cards.body: Convex lens (\(f = +20\text{ cm}\)) with \(u = -40\text{ cm}\) gives \(v_1 = +40\text{ cm}, m_1 = -1\). Concave lens (\(f = -10\text{ cm}\)) 8 cm behind has virtual object \(u_2 = +32\text{ cm}\), giving \(v \approx -14.5\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is Newton's lens formula when the same medium is on both sides?
cards.why: With the same medium on both sides, \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = f\), so \(x_1 x_2 = f_1 f_2 = -f^2\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What does a negative lateral magnification \(m < 0\) indicate?
cards.why: Since \(m = y'/y\), a negative value means \(y'\) and \(y\) have opposite signs (inverted).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A thin lens in air has \(f = 10\text{ cm}\) and \(x_1 = -20\text{ cm}\). Find \(x_2\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For a thin lens with \(u = -40\text{ cm}\) and \(v = +40\text{ cm}\), find \(m\).
cards.why: Lateral magnification \(m = v / u = (+40) / (-40) = -1\).

cards.title: Two vibrations meeting at the same point
cards.meaning: The superposition principle says that when two waves reach the same point at the same time, the total displacement is simply their sum.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="42" x2="242" y2="42" class="gk"/><line x1="18" y1="92" x2="242" y2="92" class="gk"/><line x1="18" y1="146" x2="242" y2="146" class="gk"/><path d="M 20 42 Q 45 14 70 42 T 120 42 T 170 42 T 220 42" class="lk"/><path d="M 20 92 Q 45 68 70 92 T 120 92 T 170 92 T 220 92" class="ik"/><path d="M 20 146 Q 45 98 70 146 T 120 146 T 170 146 T 220 146" class="lk"/><circle cx="45" cy="28" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="45" cy="80" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="45" cy="122" r="4" class="f"/><text x="226" y="45" class="t">x₁(t)</text><text x="226" y="95" class="t">x₂(t)</text><text x="188" y="132" class="t">x(t) = x₁ + x₂</text><text x="54" y="25" class="t">a₁</text><text x="54" y="78" class="t">a₂</text><text x="55" y="118" class="t">a₁+a₂</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the two top waves x₁(t) and x₂(t): at every instant they add up to the bottom wave x(t).
cards.example: If wave 1 pushes a particle up by 3 mm and wave 2 pushes it up by 2 mm, the particle moves up by 5 mm.
cards.bridge: For two sinusoidal waves of the same frequency ω, adding x₁(t) = a₁ cos(ωt + θ₁) and x₂(t) = a₂ cos(ωt + θ₂) gives a new sinusoidal wave x(t) = a cos(ωt + θ).

cards.label: 01 · §13.5 Definition
cards.title: What is the superposition principle for sinusoidal waves?
cards.body: When two sinusoidal waves of the same frequency superpose in the same direction, their sum x(t) = x₁(t) + x₂(t) is also simple harmonic with the same frequency ω.
cards.tex: x(t) = a_1\cos(\omega t + \theta_1) + a_2\cos(\omega t + \theta_2) = a\cos(\omega t + \theta)

cards.label: 02 · §13.5 Derivation
cards.title: Resultant amplitude of two sinusoidal waves
cards.legend: Displacements \(x_1(t) = a_1\cos(\omega t + \theta_1)\) and \(x_2(t) = a_2\cos(\omega t + \theta_2)\) with resultant \(a\cos(\omega t + \theta)\) (Eqs. 13.21–13.25, Fig. 13.8).

objects.text: a cos θ = a₁ cos θ₁ + a₂ cos θ₂
objects.name: xcomp

phases.name: Superpose
phases.why: add the two harmonic displacements x₁(t) and x₂(t)

phases.name: Components
phases.why: equate cos ωt and sin ωt parts to get a cos θ and a sin θ

phases.name: Square & add
phases.why: square and add Eqs. (13.23) and (13.24) to eliminate θ

phases.name: Cosine law
phases.why: apply the cosine difference identity and take the square root

steps.note: By superposition, the resultant displacement is \(x_1(t) + x_2(t)\) (Eq. 13.21).
Expand \(\cos(\omega t + \theta_i)\) and match coefficients of \(\cos\omega t\) (Eq. 13.23).

ask.q: How do we write the sum in harmonic form \(a\cos(\omega t + \theta)\)?
ask.why: Expanding \(\cos(\omega t + \theta)\) lets us match the \(\cos\omega t\) and \(\sin\omega t\) coefficients.

steps.note: Matching coefficients of \(-\sin\omega t\) gives the vertical component (Eq. 13.24).
Square Eqs. (13.23) and (13.24) and add them together.

ask.q: Which step eliminates the resultant phase \(\theta\) on the left?
ask.why: Squaring and adding uses \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) to isolate \(a^2\).

steps.note: Expand the squares and use \(\cos^2\theta_i + \sin^2\theta_i = 1\).

ask.q: What does \(\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2\) simplify to?
ask.why: By the cosine difference identity, \(\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2 = \cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\).

steps.note: Rewrite the cross term using \(\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\).
Take the positive square root to get the resultant amplitude (Eq. 13.25).

ask.q: When \(\theta_1 - \theta_2 = 0\), what does the resultant amplitude \(a\) equal?

cards.title: Crests boosting crests versus crests cancelling troughs
cards.meaning: Constructive interference happens when two waves arrive in step and build a tall wave; destructive interference happens when a crest meets a trough and they cancel.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="14" width="112" height="152" rx="12" class="s ok"/><rect x="136" y="14" width="112" height="152" rx="12" class="s ok"/><path d="M 22 62 Q 45 36 68 62 T 114 62" class="lk"/><path d="M 22 96 Q 45 76 68 96 T 114 96" class="ik"/><path d="M 22 138 Q 45 96 68 138 T 114 138" class="lk"/><path d="M 146 62 Q 169 36 192 62 T 238 62" class="lk"/><path d="M 146 96 Q 169 116 192 96 T 238 96" class="ik"/><line x1="146" y1="138" x2="238" y2="138" class="lk"/><text x="68" y="30" text-anchor="middle" class="t">In phase (0, 2π)</text><text x="68" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">a = a₁ + a₂</text><text x="192" y="30" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Out of phase (π)</text><text x="192" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">a = |a₁ - a₂|</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare the left box (waves in phase add to a₁ + a₂) with the right box (waves out of phase by π subtract to |a₁ - a₂|).
cards.example: Two identical waves of amplitude a give amplitude 2a when in phase and 0 when out of phase by π.
cards.bridge: Energy is never destroyed in interference: energy missing from dark destructive points is redistributed to bright constructive points.

cards.label: 03 · §13.5 Definition
cards.title: What are constructive and destructive interference?
cards.body: Constructive interference occurs when phase difference is an even multiple of π so a = a₁ + a₂; destructive interference occurs at odd multiples of π so a = |a₁ - a₂|.
cards.tex: \theta_1 \sim \theta_2 = 2n\pi \implies a = a_1 + a_2; \quad (2n+1)\pi \implies a = a_1 \sim a_2

cards.label: 04 · §§13.5–13.6 Phasor sum
cards.title: Resultant phase and N-wave graphical method (Eqs. 13.26, 13.32–13.36)
cards.body: In the graphical method (Fig. 13.8), rotating vectors of lengths \(a_1, a_2, \dots\) at angles \(\theta_1, \theta_2, \dots\) are added tip-to-tail; resultant vector \(\overrightarrow{OR}\) gives amplitude \(a\) and phase \(\theta\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When two waves with amplitudes \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) differ in phase by \(\pi\), what is \(a\)?

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In interference, total energy is conserved and is merely ______ in space.
cards.why: Interference does not violate energy conservation; energy is redistributed from minima to maxima.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Two waves of amplitudes \(3\) and \(4\) have phase difference \(\pi/2\). Find resultant amplitude \(a\).

cards.title: Tapping two points of the same wave
cards.meaning: Division of wavefront splits one incoming wave through two small openings so the two new waves stay locked in step.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="34" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><path d="M 52 54 A 45 45 0 0 1 52 126" class="gk"/><path d="M 74 40 A 68 68 0 0 1 74 140" class="lk"/><line x1="98" y1="16" x2="98" y2="54" class="ik"/><line x1="98" y1="68" x2="98" y2="112" class="ik"/><line x1="98" y1="126" x2="98" y2="164" class="ik"/><circle cx="98" cy="61" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="98" cy="119" r="3.5" class="f"/><path d="M 98 31 A 30 30 0 0 1 98 91" class="lk"/><path d="M 98 11 A 50 50 0 0 1 98 111" class="gk"/><path d="M 98 89 A 30 30 0 0 1 98 149" class="lk"/><path d="M 98 69 A 50 50 0 0 1 98 169" class="gk"/><line x1="216" y1="18" x2="216" y2="162" class="ik"/><text x="20" y="94" class="t">S</text><text x="82" y="58" class="t">S₁</text><text x="82" y="126" class="t">S₂</text><text x="182" y="28" class="t">Screen</text><text x="158" y="94" class="t">Locked phase</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at one wavefront from S hitting holes S₁ and S₂ together, launching two synchronized spherical waves.
cards.example: Because both S₁ and S₂ are fed by the exact same crest from S, any phase jump in S reaches S₁ and S₂ at the same instant.
cards.bridge: Chapter 14 studies this division of wavefront, whereas Chapter 15 studies division of amplitude at reflecting surfaces.

cards.label: 01 · §14.1 Definition
cards.title: What is division of wavefront?
cards.body: Division of wavefront is a method that divides a single wavefront into two beams using closely spaced holes, slits, mirrors, or a biprism so they keep a fixed phase relationship.

cards.title: Calm hyperbolic lanes in a ripple tank
cards.meaning: Nodal lines are curved paths in a ripple tank where a crest from one needle always meets a trough from the other needle, leaving the water still.

cards.picture: Look at the central line OZ (point A, amplitude 2a) and the curved nodal lines (point B, zero amplitude).
cards.example: At point B where S₂B - S₁B = λ/2, the wave from S₂ arrives half a cycle behind S₁ and cancels it at all times.
cards.bridge: In general, maxima lie on hyperbolas with S₂P ~ S₁P = nλ, and nodal lines (minima) lie on hyperbolas with S₂P ~ S₁P = (n + ½)λ.

cards.label: 02 · §14.2 Definition
cards.title: What are nodal lines and maxima on a water surface?
cards.body: For two in-phase point sources S₁ and S₂, points with path difference nλ form constructive maxima, while points with (n + ½)λ form destructive nodal lines of zero amplitude.

cards.label: 03 · §14.2 Derivation
cards.title: Hyperbolic equation of nodal and antinodal curves
cards.legend: Sources \(S_1(+d/2, 0)\) and \(S_2(-d/2, 0)\) on the \(x\)-axis with path difference \(S_2P - S_1P = \Delta\) at point \(P(x, z)\) (Example 14.2, Fig. 14.3).

phases.name: Distances
phases.why: express S₁P and S₂P using coordinates (x, z)

phases.name: Isolate root
phases.why: move S₁P to the right before squaring

phases.name: Square
phases.why: square both sides and simplify to 2xd - Δ²

phases.name: Hyperbola
phases.why: square again and divide into standard hyperbola form

steps.note: Start with constant path difference \(\Delta\) at point \(P(x, z)\) (Eq. 14.5).
Substitute distances from \(S_1(d/2, 0)\) and \(S_2(-d/2, 0)\) to \(P(x, z)\).

ask.q: With \(S_2\) at \((-d/2, 0)\), what is the distance \(S_2P\) to \(P(x, z)\)?
ask.why: By the distance formula from \((-d/2, 0)\) to \((x, z)\), \(S_2P = [(x + d/2)^2 + z^2]^{1/2}\).

steps.note: Add \(S_1P\) to both sides so only one square root sits on the left.

ask.q: Why isolate one square root before squaring both sides?
options: To avoid a product of two roots
ask.why: Isolating one radical leaves only a single square-root term after the first squaring.

steps.note: Square both sides of the equation.
Cancel \(x^2 + d^2/4 + z^2\) and move \(\Delta^2\) to the left.

ask.q: What does \((x + d/2)^2 - (x - d/2)^2\) simplify to?
ask.why: Expanding both squares cancels \(x^2 + d^2/4\) and leaves \(xd - (-xd) = 2xd\).

steps.note: Square both sides again and collect the \(x^2\) and \(z^2\) terms.
Divide through by the right-hand side to obtain the hyperbola (Eq. 14.6).

ask.q: What curve is described by Eq. (14.6) when \(\Delta < d\)?
ask.why: Because \(d^2 - \Delta^2 > 0\), the opposite signs on \(x^2\) and \(z^2\) define a hyperbola.

cards.label: 04 · §14.2 Example
cards.title: Intensity at path difference λ/3 (Example 14.1)
cards.tex: y = a\cos\omega t + a\cos\!\left(\omega t - \frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = 2a\cos\!\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = a\cos\!\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)
cards.body: A path difference of \(\lambda/3\) gives a phase difference of \(2\pi/3\). The resultant amplitude is \(a\), which is half the maximum amplitude \(2a\), so the intensity is \(1/4\) of \(I_{\max}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Along the perpendicular bisector of two in-phase sources of amplitude \(a\), what is the resultant amplitude?
cards.why: On the perpendicular bisector, \(S_1A = S_2A\), so waves arrive in phase and add to \(2a\) (Eq. 14.1).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the geometric shape of the nodal lines on the water surface?
cards.why: Constant path difference \(S_2P - S_1P = (n + 1/2)\lambda\) defines a family of hyperbolae (Eq. 14.6).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: At a point where \(S_2P - S_1P = \lambda/3\), find \(I / I_{\max}\) as a decimal.

cards.title: Why two separate sodium lamps never show fringes
cards.meaning: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference, whereas independent lamps emit short random atomic bursts whose phase jumps every ten-billionth of a second.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="14" width="110" height="152" rx="12" class="s ok"/><rect x="136" y="14" width="110" height="152" rx="12" class="s ok"/><circle cx="34" cy="58" r="5" class="f"/><circle cx="34" cy="118" r="5" class="f"/><line x1="62" y1="34" x2="62" y2="142" class="ik"/><circle cx="62" cy="58" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="62" cy="118" r="3" class="f"/><line x1="108" y1="34" x2="108" y2="142" class="lk"/><text x="69" y="30" text-anchor="middle" class="t">2 lamps (incoherent)</text><text x="69" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">φ jumps in 10⁻¹⁰ s</text><text x="69" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Uniform I = 2I₀</text><circle cx="154" cy="88" r="4" class="f"/><line x1="182" y1="34" x2="182" y2="142" class="ik"/><circle cx="182" cy="62" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="182" cy="114" r="3" class="f"/><line x1="230" y1="34" x2="230" y2="142" class="lk"/><circle cx="230" cy="52" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="230" cy="88" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="230" cy="124" r="3" class="f"/><text x="191" y="30" text-anchor="middle" class="t">1 pinhole S (coherent)</text><text x="191" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Fixed δ</text><text x="191" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Fringes: 4I₀ cos²(δ/2)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare two independent lamps on the left (uniform 2I₀) with Young's single pinhole S feeding S₁ and S₂ on the right (stationary fringes).
cards.example: Atoms emit light pulses lasting ~10⁻¹⁰ s. Over the eye's 0.1 s response time, ⟨cos²(φ/2)⟩ averages to 1/2, giving uniform intensity 2I₀.
cards.bridge: Young solved this in 1801 by illuminating two close pinholes S₁ and S₂ from a single pinhole S so their phase difference stays locked.

cards.label: 01 · §§14.3–14.4 Definition
cards.title: What are coherent and incoherent sources?
cards.body: Coherent sources maintain a fixed phase relationship over time and form stationary fringes; incoherent sources have a phase difference that varies randomly in ~10⁻¹⁰ s, giving uniform intensity I₁ + I₂.

cards.title: Equally spaced bright and dark bands on a distant screen
cards.meaning: Fringe width β is the constant step size from one bright band to the next on Young's screen.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="46" y1="22" x2="46" y2="158" class="ik"/><line x1="204" y1="16" x2="204" y2="164" class="lk"/><line x1="46" y1="90" x2="204" y2="90" class="gk"/><circle cx="46" cy="68" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="46" cy="112" r="4" class="f"/><line x1="46" y1="68" x2="204" y2="42" class="lk"/><line x1="46" y1="112" x2="204" y2="42" class="ik"/><circle cx="204" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="66" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="42" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="114" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="138" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="28" y="72" class="t">S₁</text><text x="28" y="116" class="t">S₂</text><text x="28" y="94" class="t">d</text><text x="125" y="152" text-anchor="middle" class="t">D ≫ d</text><text x="216" y="94" class="t">O (n=0)</text><text x="216" y="70" class="t">x₁ = β</text><text x="216" y="46" class="t">P (x_n)</text><text x="144" y="30" text-anchor="middle" class="t">β = λD/d</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at screen LL' on the right: when D ≫ d, bright fringes sit at evenly spaced multiples of β = λD/d.
cards.example: For d = 0.02 cm, D = 50 cm, and λ = 6 × 10⁻⁵ cm, the fringe width is β = λD/d = 0.15 cm.
cards.bridge: Near the center (y² ≪ D²), the hyperbolic loci look like parallel straight lines and are non-localized in space.

cards.label: 02 · §14.5 Definition
cards.title: What is fringe width in Young's experiment?
cards.body: Fringe width β is the constant distance between any two successive bright or dark fringes on a screen at distance D from two coherent sources separated by d.

cards.label: 03 · §14.5 Derivation
cards.title: Path difference and fringe width in Young's experiment
cards.legend: Pinholes \(S_1, S_2\) separated by \(d\), screen \(LL'\) at distance \(D \gg d, x_n\), point \(P\) at distance \(OP = x_n\) (Eqs. 14.17–14.21, Fig. 14.8).

phases.name: Right triangles
phases.why: write (S₂P)² - (S₁P)² from screen distance D and height x_n

phases.name: Factor
phases.why: use difference of squares to isolate S₂P - S₁P

phases.name: Paraxial
phases.why: replace S₂P + S₁P by 2D when D ≫ d, x_n

phases.name: Fringe width
phases.why: set path difference equal to nλ and subtract adjacent maxima

steps.note: Use the Pythagorean theorem for \(S_2P\) and \(S_1P\) (Eq. 14.18).
Expand the squares; \(D^2 + x_n^2 + d^2/4\) cancels out.

ask.q: What remains on the right after \(D^2 + x_n^2 + d^2/4\) cancels?

steps.note: Factor the left-hand side as a difference of squares.
Divide both sides by \(S_2P + S_1P\).

ask.q: When \(D \gg d, x_n\), what accurately approximates \(S_2P + S_1P\)?
ask.why: Since \(S_1P \approx D\) and \(S_2P \approx D\), their sum is very nearly \(2D\).

steps.note: Replace \(S_2P + S_1P\) with \(2D\) and cancel the factor of 2 (Eq. 14.19).
Set the path difference equal to \(n\lambda\) for the \(n\)-th bright fringe (Eq. 14.17).

ask.q: For constructive interference at \(P\), what must \(S_2P - S_1P\) equal?
ask.why: Bright fringes occur where the path difference is an integer multiple \(n\lambda\).

steps.note: Multiply both sides by \(D/d\) to find the bright fringe position (Eq. 14.20).
Subtract \(x_n\) from \(x_{n+1}\) to obtain the fringe width (Eq. 14.21).

ask.q: How does fringe width \(\beta\) change if screen distance \(D\) is doubled?
ask.why: Since \(\beta = \lambda D / d\), doubling \(D\) doubles the fringe width \(\beta\).

cards.label: 04 · §14.6 Derivation
cards.title: Two-beam interference intensity distribution
cards.legend: Electric fields \(E_1, E_2\) with intensities \(I_1, I_2\) and phase difference \(\delta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}(S_2P - S_1P)\) (Eqs. 14.27–14.33).

phases.name: Time average
phases.why: average the squared resultant field over detector response time τ

phases.name: Interference term
phases.why: write I in terms of I₁, I₂, and phase difference δ

phases.name: Equal beams
phases.why: set I₁ = I₂ = I₀ for two equal pinholes

phases.name: Cos-squared law
phases.why: apply 1 + cos δ = 2 cos²(δ/2)

steps.note: Intensity recorded by a detector is proportional to the time average of \(E^2\) (Eq. 14.27).
Use \(\langle\cos^2(\omega t - \theta)\rangle = 1/2\) and \(\langle\cos(2\omega t - \theta)\rangle = 0\) (Eq. 14.30).

ask.q: Over detector time \(\tau \gg T\), what is \(\langle\cos^2(\omega t - \theta)\rangle\)?
ask.why: Since \(\omega \approx 10^{15}\text{ s}^{-1}\), \(\cos^2(\omega t - \theta)\) averages to \(1/2\) (Eq. 14.29).

steps.note: For two equal sources \(I_1 = I_2 = I_0\), both terms equal \(2I_0\).

ask.q: For unequal intensities \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), what is \(I_{\max}\)?
ask.why: Setting \(\cos\delta = +1\) in Eq. (14.30) gives \(I_{\max} = (\sqrt{I_1} + \sqrt{I_2})^2\) (Eq. 14.32).

steps.note: Factor out \(2I_0\) on the right-hand side.

ask.q: Which half-angle identity replaces \(1 + \cos\delta\)?
ask.why: By trigonometry, \(1 + \cos\delta = 2\cos^2(\delta/2)\).

steps.note: This gives the \(\cos^2(\delta/2)\) intensity distribution (Eq. 14.33).

ask.q: At destructive minima \(\delta = (2n + 1)\pi\), what is \(I\) when \(I_1 = I_2 = I_0\)?
ask.why: At odd multiples of \(\pi\), \(\cos(\delta/2) = 0\), so \(I_{\min} = 0\).

cards.label: 05 · §14.6 Graph
cards.title: The cos²(δ/2) intensity distribution (Fig. 14.9)
cards.body: For two equal coherent beams, intensity varies as I = 4I₀ cos²(δ/2), reaching maxima 4I₀ at δ = 0, ±2π, ±4π and zero minima at δ = ±π, ±3π, ±5π.

cards.label: 06 · §14.6 Examples
cards.title: Two plane waves & circular fringes on a normal screen (Examples 14.5–14.6)
cards.body: Two plane waves at symmetric angles \(\pm\theta\) form straight fringes of width \(\lambda/(2\sin\theta)\). On a screen perpendicular to line \(S_1S_2\) (Fig. 14.12), fringes are concentric circles.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: On a screen perpendicular to the line joining \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), what is the fringe shape?
cards.why: By rotational symmetry around the axis joining \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), constant \(S_1P - S_2P\) gives circles (Example 14.6).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Young's double-hole fringes can be seen anywhere in space and are called ______ fringes.
cards.why: Point or slit sources form fringes throughout the overlapping region without needing a focusing lens.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Find \(\beta\) in mm for \(\lambda = 5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mm}\), \(D = 500\text{ mm}\), and \(d = 0.5\text{ mm}\).
cards.why: \(\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d} = \frac{5 \times 10^{-4} \times 500}{0.5} = 0.5\text{ mm}\) (Problem 14.1).

cards.title: Splitting one slit into two virtual slits with two mirrors
cards.meaning: Fresnel's two-mirror arrangement reflects light from one slit off two nearly flat mirrors touching at angle θ so the two reflections act as coherent virtual sources.
cards.picture: Look at slit S and its two virtual images S₁ and S₂ on the circle centered at mirror junction M.
cards.example: Because S, S₁, and S₂ all lie at distance R from junction M, angle S₁MS₂ is 2θ and the virtual slit separation is d = 2Rθ.
cards.bridge: In the overlapping region BC on the screen, the reflected wavefronts from M₁M and MM₂ interfere to form straight fringes.

cards.label: 01 · §14.7 Definition
cards.title: What is Fresnel's two-mirror arrangement?
cards.body: Fresnel's two-mirror arrangement consists of two plane mirrors M₁M and MM₂ inclined at a small angle θ, producing two coherent virtual images S₁ and S₂ separated by d = 2Rθ.

cards.title: A razor-thin double prism that bends one slit into two
cards.meaning: Fresnel's biprism is a single glass prism with tiny base angles α (~20') that refracts the upper and lower halves of a wavefront into two virtual slits S₁ and S₂.
