cards.picture: Look at the thin biprism at distance a from slit S: refraction creates two coherent virtual slits S₁ and S₂.
cards.example: For n = 1.5, α = 20' ≈ 5.8 × 10⁻³ rad, and a = 2 cm, the virtual slit separation is d = 2a(n - 1)α ≈ 0.012 cm.
cards.bridge: Putting a convex lens at two conjugate positions L₁ and L₂ between the biprism and eyepiece lets us measure d = √(d₁d₂) without measuring α.

cards.label: 02 · §14.8 Definition
cards.title: What is Fresnel's biprism?
cards.body: Fresnel's biprism is a prism with two very small base angles α (~20') that refracts light from a slit S at distance a into two coherent virtual sources separated by d = 2a(n - 1)α.

cards.label: 03 · §14.8 Derivation
cards.title: Virtual slit separation and wavelength in Fresnel's biprism
cards.legend: Biprism of refractive index \(n\) and acute angle \(\alpha\) at distance \(a\) from slit \(S\), total screen distance \(D\) (Eq. 14.34, Fig. 14.19).

phases.name: Prism deviation
phases.why: find angular deviation δ of each thin half-prism

phases.name: Virtual slits
phases.why: project both deviated beams back by distance a

phases.name: Total distance
phases.why: write fringe width β on the eyepiece crosswires

phases.name: Wavelength
phases.why: solve for λ in terms of d, β, and D

steps.note: Each half of the biprism is a thin prism of small angle \(\alpha\) that deviates rays by \((n - 1)\alpha\).

move.label: Project both deviated rays back by distance a

steps.note: At distance \(a\) behind the biprism, the two virtual images \(S_1, S_2\) are separated by \(2a\delta\).

ask.q: If each half-prism shifts its image by \(a(n - 1)\alpha\), what is \(d = S_1 S_2\)?
ask.why: The two virtual images are displaced symmetrically above and below \(S\), giving \(d = 2a(n - 1)\alpha\).

move.label: Write fringe width β on the eyepiece crosswires

steps.note: At total distance \(D\) from \(S_1 S_2\) to the crosswires \(C\), fringe width is \(\beta = \lambda D / d\).

ask.q: In the displacement method with lens positions \(L_1, L_2\), what does \(D\) equal?
ask.why: By conjugate symmetry of the two lens positions, \(D = b_1 + b_2\).

steps.note: Multiply both sides by \(d / D\).

ask.q: How do we isolate wavelength \(\lambda\) from \(\beta = \lambda D / d\)?
ask.why: Multiplying by \(d/D\) cancels \(D/d\) on the right and leaves \(\lambda = d\beta / D\).

steps.note: Swap sides to obtain the biprism wavelength relation (Eq. 14.34).

ask.q: How is \(d\) found from image separations \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) at \(L_1, L_2\)?
ask.why: Since the two lens positions have reciprocal magnifications, \(d = \sqrt{d_1 d_2}\).

cards.label: 04 · §14.8 Example
cards.title: Typical Fresnel biprism parameters (§14.8)
cards.body: For \(n = 1.5\), \(\alpha = 20' \approx 5.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ rad}\), and \(a = 2\text{ cm}\), \(d \approx 0.012\text{ cm}\). With \(D \approx 50\text{ cm}\) and \(\lambda \approx 6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\), fringe width is \(\beta \approx 0.3\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Fresnel's two-mirror setup with mirror angle \(\theta\) and \(MS = R\), what is \(S_1S_2\)?
cards.why: Since \(S, S_1, S_2\) lie on a circle of radius \(R\) and \(\angle S_1 M S_2 = 2\theta\), \(S_1S_2 = 2R\theta\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why is a narrow slit used instead of a point source in Fresnel's biprism?
options: To eliminate the need for an eyepiece
To double the wavelength of light
cards.why: Each pair of points along the slit forms overlapping straight fringes, greatly increasing brightness.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In the biprism lens method, \(d_1 = 0.04\text{ cm}\) and \(d_2 = 0.01\text{ cm}\). Find \(d\) in cm.
cards.why: From \(d = \sqrt{d_1 d_2}\), \(d = \sqrt{0.04 \times 0.01} = 0.02\text{ cm}\).

cards.title: Why white light gives one white center and a few colored fringes
cards.meaning: At the center O every color has zero path difference and adds up to white, while slightly away different colors cancel at different places.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="18" y="18" width="224" height="144" rx="14" class="s ok"/><line x1="34" y1="90" x2="226" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="34" y1="68" x2="226" y2="68" class="ik"/><line x1="34" y1="112" x2="226" y2="112" class="ik"/><line x1="34" y1="48" x2="226" y2="48" class="gk"/><line x1="34" y1="132" x2="226" y2="132" class="gk"/><circle cx="52" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="52" cy="68" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="52" cy="48" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="66" y="94" class="t">O: Δ = 0 → White central fringe</text><text x="66" y="72" class="t">P: Δ = λ_v/2 → Reddish (no violet)</text><text x="66" y="52" class="t">Q: Δ = λ_r/2 → Violet (no red)</text><text x="130" y="152" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Far from O (R): uniform white illumination</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at O (white center), P (violet absent → reddish), Q (red absent → violet), and far away R (uniform white).
cards.example: At Δ = 2 × 10⁻⁵ cm = λ_violet/2, violet light (4 × 10⁻⁵ cm) cancels completely, leaving a reddish fringe.
cards.bridge: With monochromatic sodium light all fringes look alike, so white light is used to pinpoint the zero-order central fringe.

cards.label: 01 · §14.9 Definition
cards.title: What is the white-light interference pattern?
cards.body: With white light, zero path difference at O produces a white central fringe, flanked by a few colored fringes (reddish then violet) that quickly overlap into uniform white.

cards.label: 02 · §14.10 Derivation
cards.title: Displacement of fringes by a thin transparent plate
cards.legend: Thin plate of thickness \(t\) and index \(n\) placed in front of \(S_1\), shifting the central fringe from \(O\) to \(O'\) by \(\Delta = OO'\) (Eqs. 14.35–14.37, Fig. 14.20).

phases.name: Travel time
phases.why: sum travel time (S₁P - t)/c in air and t/v in the plate

phases.name: Optical path
phases.why: substitute v = c/n to find extra optical path (n - 1)t

phases.name: Central fringe
phases.why: equate optical paths at the shifted central fringe O'

phases.name: Fringe shift
phases.why: use S₂O' - S₁O' = d Δ / D to solve for shift Δ

steps.note: Light from \(S_1\) travels distance \(t\) in the plate at speed \(v\) and \(S_1P - t\) in air at speed \(c\).
Since \(t/v = nt/c\), the effective optical path increases by \((n - 1)t\) (Eq. 14.35).

ask.q: By how much does a plate of thickness \(t\) and index \(n\) increase optical path?
ask.why: Replacing air of thickness \(t\) by medium \(n\) adds \(nt - t = (n - 1)t\) to the optical path.

move.label: Equate optical paths from S₁ and S₂ at O'

steps.note: The central fringe shifts to \(O'\) where optical paths from \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are equal.

ask.q: At the new central fringe \(O'\), how do the two optical paths compare?
ask.why: The zero-order central fringe always forms where total optical path difference is zero.

steps.note: Subtract \(S_1O'\) from both sides.
Use Eq. (14.19) with \(OO' = \Delta\) so \(S_2O' - S_1O' = (d/D)\Delta\) (Eq. 14.36).

ask.q: For displacement \(\Delta = OO'\), what does \(S_2O' - S_1O'\) equal?
ask.why: By Eq. (14.19), geometric path difference at height \(\Delta\) is \((d/D)\Delta\).

steps.note: Multiply both sides by \(D/d\).
Swap sides to get the fringe displacement formula (Eq. 14.37).

ask.q: When the plate covers \(S_1\), which way does the central fringe shift?
ask.why: To make \(S_2O' > S_1O'\), \(O'\) must lie on the side of the covered slit \(S_1\).

cards.title: Grazing reflection that turns the central fringe dark
cards.meaning: Lloyd's mirror lets direct light from a slit S₁ interfere with light reflected at a grazing angle from a flat mirror, revealing a sudden π phase flip on reflection.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="68" y1="110" x2="156" y2="110" class="lk"/><line x1="156" y1="24" x2="156" y2="156" class="gk"/><line x1="218" y1="24" x2="218" y2="156" class="ik"/><circle cx="34" cy="92" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="34" cy="128" r="3.5" class="f"/><line x1="34" y1="92" x2="218" y2="68" class="lk"/><line x1="34" y1="92" x2="118" y2="110" class="ik"/><line x1="118" y1="110" x2="218" y2="68" class="ik"/><line x1="34" y1="128" x2="118" y2="110" class="gk"/><circle cx="218" cy="68" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="16" y="95" class="t">S₁</text><text x="16" y="132" class="t">S₂</text><text x="112" y="126" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Mirror (π shift)</text><text x="156" y="18" text-anchor="middle" class="t">L₁'</text><text x="218" y="18" text-anchor="middle" class="t">L₁</text><text x="228" y="72" class="t">P</text><text x="156" y="168" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Dark at contact</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at direct ray S₁P and mirror-reflected ray (as if from virtual slit S₂): when screen L₁'L₂' touches the mirror end, the contact fringe is dark.
cards.example: Because reflection at the denser mirror adds a phase shift of π, integer path differences S₂P - S₁P = nλ give dark minima instead of bright maxima.
cards.bridge: In §14.12, optical reversibility (Stokes' relations) proves that if denser reflection has a π phase shift, rarer reflection has none.

cards.label: 03 · §14.11 Definition
cards.title: What is Lloyd's mirror arrangement?
cards.body: Lloyd's mirror interferes direct light from slit S₁ with light reflected at grazing incidence from a mirror; its dark central fringe proves a π phase shift on denser reflection.

cards.title: Running a reflected and refracted ray backward in time
cards.meaning: Stokes' relations come from running light backward: reversing the reflected and transmitted rays must rebuild the original incident ray and cancel any extra ray.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="14" y1="90" x2="118" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="142" y1="90" x2="246" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="26" y1="42" x2="66" y2="90" class="ik"/><line x1="66" y1="90" x2="106" y2="42" class="lk"/><line x1="66" y1="90" x2="96" y2="144" class="lk"/><line x1="234" y1="42" x2="194" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="224" y1="144" x2="194" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="194" y1="90" x2="154" y2="42" class="ik"/><line x1="194" y1="90" x2="164" y2="144" class="gk"/><text x="32" y="36" class="t">a</text><text x="102" y="36" class="t">ar₁</text><text x="98" y="152" class="t">at₁</text><text x="24" y="80" class="t">n₁</text><text x="24" y="106" class="t">n₂</text><text x="148" y="32" class="t">ar₁²+at₁t₂ = a</text><text x="144" y="162" class="t">at₁r₂+ar₁t₁ = 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare (a) on the left (incident ray a splits into ar₁ and at₁) with time-reversed (b) on the right (rebuilds a and cancels to 0 in n₂).
cards.example: Cancelling the unwanted downward ray in medium n₂ gives at₁r₂ + ar₁t₁ = 0, so r₂ = -r₁.
cards.bridge: Since r₂ = -r₁, the opposite signs mean a π phase shift on denser reflection and zero phase shift on rarer reflection.

cards.label: 04 · §14.12 Definition
cards.title: What are Stokes' relations?
cards.body: Stokes' relations are t₁t₂ = 1 - r₁² and r₂ = -r₁, derived from optical reversibility for amplitude reflection (r₁, r₂) and transmission (t₁, t₂) coefficients.

cards.label: 05 · §14.12 Derivation
cards.title: Stokes' relations from optical reversibility
cards.legend: Incident amplitude \(a\), reflection and transmission coefficients \(r_1, t_1\) (from \(n_1\) to \(n_2\)) and \(r_2, t_2\) (from \(n_2\) to \(n_1\)) (Eqs. 14.38–14.39, Fig. 14.22).

phases.name: Retrace incident
phases.why: reversing ar₁ and at₁ must reconstruct incident amplitude a

phases.name: First Stokes law
phases.why: divide by a and isolate t₁t₂

phases.name: Cancel second ray
phases.why: equate the net amplitude along the absent direction in n₂ to zero

phases.name: Second Stokes law
phases.why: divide by a t₁ to obtain r₂ = -r₁

steps.note: By optical reversibility, reversed rays \(ar_1^2\) and \(at_1 t_2\) combine to give \(a\) (Fig. 14.22b).
Divide both sides by incident amplitude \(a\).

ask.q: Which principle states that reversed rays retrace the original path?
ask.why: In the absence of absorption, time-reversal invariance ensures optical reversibility.

steps.note: Subtract \(r_1^2\) to obtain the first Stokes' relation (Eq. 14.38).

move.label: Equate reversed amplitudes in medium 2 to zero

steps.note: In medium \(n_2\), rays \(at_1 r_2\) and \(ar_1 t_1\) must cancel completely.

ask.q: Why must \(at_1 r_2 + ar_1 t_1\) equal zero in Fig. 14.22(b)?
options: No such ray existed in Fig. 14.22(a)
ask.why: Time reversal of Fig. 14.22(a) has no outgoing ray along that direction in medium \(n_2\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(at_1\).

ask.q: Which common factor is divided out of \(at_1 r_2 + ar_1 t_1 = 0\)?
ask.why: Both terms contain the non-zero transmitted amplitude \(at_1\).

steps.note: Subtract \(r_1\) to obtain the second Stokes' relation (Eq. 14.39).

ask.q: Since denser reflection has a \(\pi\) phase shift, what does \(r_2 = -r_1\) imply for rarer reflection?
ask.why: The minus sign accounts for the \(\pi\) shift on the denser side, so the rarer side has zero shift.

cards.label: 06 · §14.10 Examples
cards.title: Mica sheet thickness from fringe shift (Examples 14.10–14.11)
cards.body: For \(n = 1.58, d = 0.1\text{ cm}, D = 50\text{ cm}, \Delta = 0.2\text{ cm}\), \(t \approx 6.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ cm}\). If the central fringe shifts to the 11th bright fringe, \(0.58t = 11\lambda\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why is the central fringe in Young's experiment white when white light is used?
options: All wavelengths have zero path difference at \(O\)
Refractive index of air is zero
cards.why: At \(O\), \(S_2O = S_1O\) for every wavelength, so all colors interfere constructively.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the central fringe at the mirror contact point in Lloyd's mirror?
options: Dark due to a \(\pi\) phase shift
Bright due to zero path difference
cards.why: Reflection at the denser mirror introduces an abrupt phase shift of \(\pi\), making the contact point dark.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A sheet with \(n = 1.5\) shifts fringes by \(5\lambda\) for \(\lambda = 0.5\,\mu\text{m}\). Find \(t\) in \(\mu\text{m}\).
cards.why: From \((n - 1)t = 5\lambda\), \(0.5t = 2.5\,\mu\text{m}\), so \(t = 5\,\mu\text{m}\).

cards.title: Splitting one wave at the top and bottom of a thin film
cards.meaning: Division of amplitude splits an incoming wave into two reflections — one from the top surface of a thin film and one from the bottom surface — that then interfere.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="24" y="92" width="212" height="52" class="s ok"/><line x1="34" y1="24" x2="82" y2="92" class="ik"/><line x1="82" y1="92" x2="138" y2="20" class="lk"/><line x1="82" y1="92" x2="114" y2="144" class="lk"/><line x1="114" y1="144" x2="146" y2="92" class="lk"/><line x1="146" y1="92" x2="202" y2="20" class="ik"/><line x1="146" y1="92" x2="112" y2="65" class="gk"/><text x="42" y="84" class="t">n₁ (air)</text><text x="42" y="122" class="t">n₂, d</text><text x="80" y="104" class="t">B</text><text x="110" y="158" class="t">D</text><text x="150" y="104" class="t">F</text><text x="102" y="58" class="t">C</text><text x="176" y="122" class="t">Δ = 2n₂d cos θ'</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at incident ray hitting B: the upper reflection and the lower reflection (via B–D–F) travel side by side with optical path difference Δ = 2n₂d cos θ'.
cards.example: At normal incidence (θ' = 0, cos θ' = 1) on a film in air, the extra optical path is 2nd and the upper reflection shifts phase by π.
cards.bridge: When the film index lies between the two surrounding media (like oil on flint glass or MgF₂ on glass), both reflections shift phase by π.

cards.label: 01 · §§15.1–15.3 Definition
cards.title: What is division of amplitude and the cosine law?
cards.body: In division of amplitude at a plane parallel film of thickness d and index n₂, the lower reflection travels an extra optical path Δ = 2n₂d cos θ' given by the cosine law.
cards.tex: \Delta = 2n_2 d\cos\theta' = m\lambda \;(\text{minima in air}), \quad \left(m + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda \;(\text{maxima in air})
examples: Film in air: π shift at top
n₁ < n₂ < n₃: π at both

cards.label: 02 · §15.3 Derivation
cards.title: The cosine law for a plane parallel thin film
cards.legend: Film of thickness \(d\) and index \(n_2\) in medium \(n_1\), incidence angle \(\theta\), refraction angle \(\theta'\), image point \(B'\) at depth \(2d\) (Eqs. 15.3–15.9, Fig. 15.5).

phases.name: Optical path
phases.why: write extra optical path Δ = n₂(BD + DF) - n₁ BC

phases.name: Image point B'
phases.why: extend BJ = JB' = d so BD + DF = B'F

phases.name: Snell's law
phases.why: express n₁ BC as n₂ KF using Snell's law

phases.name: Cosine law
phases.why: replace B'F - KF with B'K = 2d cos θ'

steps.note: Start with the optical path difference between the lower and upper reflections (Eq. 15.3).
Reflect \(B\) across the lower surface to \(B'\) so \(BD = B'D\) and \(BD + DF = B'F\) (Eq. 15.7).

ask.q: Since \(BJ = JB' = d\), why does \(BD + DF\) equal \(B'F\)?
ask.why: Right triangles \(BDJ\) and \(B'DJ\) give \(BD = B'D\), so \(B'D + DF = B'F\).

steps.note: Since \(BC = BF\sin\theta\) and \(KF = BF\sin\theta'\), Snell's law gives \(n_1 BC = n_2 KF\) (Eq. 15.8).

ask.q: Using \(BC = BF\sin\theta\) and \(KF = BF\sin\theta'\), what does \(n_1 BC\) equal?
ask.why: By Snell's law \(n_1\sin\theta = n_2\sin\theta'\), so \(n_1 BC = n_1 BF\sin\theta = n_2 BF\sin\theta' = n_2 KF\).

steps.note: Factor out \(n_2\) on the right-hand side.
Since \(K\) lies on segment \(B'F\), \(B'F - KF = B'K\).

ask.q: Along straight line \(B'KF\), what segment equals \(B'F - KF\)?
ask.why: Point \(K\) divides \(B'F\) into \(B'K\) and \(KF\), so \(B'F - KF = B'K\).

steps.note: In right triangle \(BB'K\) with \(BB' = 2d\), \(B'K = 2d\cos\theta'\) (Eq. 15.9, the cosine law).

ask.q: In right triangle \(BB'K\) with hypotenuse \(BB' = 2d\), what is \(B'K\)?
ask.why: Side \(B'K\) is adjacent to angle \(\angle BB'K = \theta'\) and hypotenuse \(BB' = 2d\).

cards.title: Making glass invisible by cancelling its own reflection
cards.meaning: A non-reflecting film is a quarter-wavelength coating on glass whose top and bottom reflections are equal in strength and opposite in phase, so they cancel out.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="24" y="72" width="212" height="42" class="s ok"/><rect x="24" y="114" width="212" height="46" class="s ok"/><line x1="56" y1="18" x2="76" y2="72" class="ik"/><line x1="76" y1="72" x2="98" y2="18" class="lk"/><line x1="76" y1="72" x2="96" y2="114" class="lk"/><line x1="96" y1="114" x2="116" y2="72" class="lk"/><line x1="116" y1="72" x2="138" y2="18" class="ik"/><text x="184" y="58" class="t">Air (n_a = 1)</text><text x="184" y="96" class="t">Film (n_f < n_g)</text><text x="184" y="140" class="t">Glass (n_g)</text><text x="46" y="34" class="t">(1)</text><text x="94" y="34" class="t">(2)</text><text x="142" y="34" class="t">(5)</text><text x="28" y="96" class="t">d = λ/(4n_f)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at reflected rays (2) and (5): both reflect off denser media (π shift each), and the extra path 2n_f d = λ/2 puts them out of phase.
cards.example: Uncoated crown glass (n = 1.5) reflects 4% at each surface; a λ/(4n_f) MgF₂ film (n_f = 1.38) cuts reflection to 1.3% (blooming).
cards.bridge: Complete cancellation occurs when 2n_f d = λ/2 (so d = λ/(4n_f)) and the two reflected amplitudes match, giving n_f = √(n_a n_g).

cards.label: 03 · §15.4 Definition
cards.title: What is a non-reflecting film (blooming)?
cards.body: A non-reflecting film is a dielectric layer of index n_f between air (n_a) and glass (n_g) and thickness d = λ/(4n_f) that cancels reflected waves by destructive interference.

cards.label: 04 · §15.4 Derivation
cards.title: Thickness and refractive index of a non-reflecting film
cards.legend: Air index \(n_a\), film index \(n_f\), glass index \(n_g\) with \(n_a < n_f < n_g\) at near-normal incidence (Eqs. 15.15–15.18, Fig. 15.7).

phases.name: Destructive phase
phases.why: equate round-trip optical path 2n_f d to half a wavelength

phases.name: Quarter-wave
phases.why: divide by 2n_f to find minimum film thickness d

phases.name: Equal amplitudes
phases.why: equate upper and lower reflected amplitudes for complete cancellation

phases.name: Optimal index
phases.why: cross-multiply and solve for n_f

steps.note: Since \(n_a < n_f < n_g\), both reflections shift phase by \(\pi\), so destructive interference requires \(2n_f d = \lambda/2\).
Divide by \(2n_f\) to get the quarter-wave film thickness (Eq. 15.15).

ask.q: Why does destructive interference occur at \(2n_f d = \lambda/2\) instead of \(\lambda\)?
options: Both interfaces suffer a \(\pi\) phase shift
Neither interface has a phase shift
Only the glass interface shifts phase
Light speeds up inside the film
ask.why: Because \(n_a < n_f < n_g\), both reflections are at denser media and their \(\pi\) shifts cancel.

move.label: Equate reflected amplitudes of rays (2) and (5) (Eq. 15.17)

steps.note: For complete cancellation (with \(4n_a n_f/(n_f+n_a)^2 \approx 1\)), equate the two Fresnel reflection coefficients (Eq. 15.17).

ask.q: For complete destructive interference, what must be true of rays (2) and (5)?
ask.why: Two out-of-phase waves cancel completely only when their amplitudes are equal.

steps.note: Cross-multiply by \((n_f + n_a)(n_g + n_f)\).

steps.tex: n_f^2 - n_a n_g = n_a n_g - n_f^2
steps.note: Expand both sides and cancel \(n_f n_g - n_a n_f\).

ask.q: When both products are expanded, which terms cancel from both sides?
ask.why: Both sides contain \(+n_f n_g - n_a n_f\), leaving \(n_f^2 - n_a n_g = n_a n_g - n_f^2\).

steps.note: Collect \(2n_f^2 = 2n_a n_g\) and divide by 2.
Take the square root to obtain the ideal anti-reflective film index (Eq. 15.18).

ask.q: For crown glass (\(n_g = 1.5\)) in air (\(n_a = 1\)), what is the ideal \(n_f\)?

cards.label: 05 · §15.4.2 Graph
cards.title: Reflectivity R(δ) of an anti-reflecting film (Fig. 15.9)
cards.body: For n_a = 1, n_g = 1.5, and n_f = √1.5 ≈ 1.225, reflectivity R drops to zero at δ = π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2 (d = λ/4n_f, 3λ/4n_f). A λ/4n_f film is used because R(λ) stays lowest across visible wavelengths.

cards.label: 06 · §15.4 Worked calculation
cards.title: MgF₂ non-reflecting coating thickness & reflectivity (§15.4)
cards.tex: d = \frac{5.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}}{4 \times 1.38} \approx 0.9 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}, \quad R = \left(\frac{n_a n_g - n_f^2}{n_a n_g + n_f^2}\right)^2 \approx 1.3\%
cards.body: For \(\lambda = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\) and \(\text{MgF}_2\) (\(n_f = 1.38\)) on crown glass (\(n_g = 1.5\)), thickness is \(d \approx 0.9 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\) and reflectivity drops from \(4\%\) to \(1.3\%\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For a film of index \(n_2 = 1.60\) between crown glass (1.52) and flint glass (1.66) at normal incidence, when do maxima occur?
cards.why: Since \(1.52 < 1.60 < 1.66\), a \(\pi\) phase shift occurs at both interfaces, so \(2nd = m\lambda\) gives maxima (Eq. 15.2b).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Reducing lens surface reflectivity with a thin quarter-wave coating is called ______.
cards.why: Coating a lens with a \(\lambda/(4n_f)\) film to reduce reflection losses is known as blooming (§15.4).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Find the minimum non-reflecting thickness \(d\) in nm for \(\lambda = 552\text{ nm}\) and \(n_f = 1.38\).

cards.title: Contour lines of constant thickness on a soap film or wedge
cards.meaning: Fringes of equal thickness are bright and dark bands that trace out places where a thin film has the exact same thickness.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="24,132 232,132 232,76" class="s ok"/><line x1="24" y1="132" x2="236" y2="132" class="ik"/><line x1="24" y1="132" x2="232" y2="76" class="lk"/><line x1="76" y1="28" x2="76" y2="132" class="gk"/><line x1="128" y1="28" x2="128" y2="132" class="gk"/><line x1="180" y1="28" x2="180" y2="132" class="gk"/><circle cx="76" cy="118" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="128" cy="104" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="180" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="76" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">t = λ/2</text><text x="128" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">t = λ</text><text x="180" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">t = 3λ/2</text><text x="130" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Each fringe = locus of constant thickness t</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the thin wedge film: each vertical line marks a thickness t = mλ/2 where a dark fringe forms.
cards.example: When sunlight hits a soap bubble or oil film on water, different colors constructively interfere at different thicknesses, painting colored contour bands.
cards.bridge: If the film is thicker than a few wavelengths, many colors overlap at every point and the white-light fringes wash out.

cards.label: 01 · §15.9 Definition
cards.title: What are fringes of equal thickness and thin-film colors?
cards.body: In a thin film of varying thickness illuminated by an extended source, each fringe follows a locus of constant film thickness; white light produces colored fringes if the film is very thin.

objects.text: Constant thickness t along each fringe
objects.name: film

cards.title: Circular air-film fringes under a curved lens
cards.meaning: Newton's rings are concentric dark and bright circles formed because the air gap between a spherical lens and a flat glass plate has constant thickness around each circle.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M 22 48 Q 92 128 162 48 Z" class="s ok"/><line x1="18" y1="88" x2="166" y2="88" class="ik"/><line x1="92" y1="22" x2="92" y2="88" class="gk"/><line x1="132" y1="72" x2="132" y2="88" class="lk"/><circle cx="92" cy="88" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="6" class="f"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="16" class="lk"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="24" class="ik"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="31" class="lk"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="37" class="ik"/><text x="92" y="104" text-anchor="middle" class="t">O (t=0)</text><text x="112" y="104" text-anchor="middle" class="t">r_m</text><text x="142" y="82" class="t">t</text><text x="78" y="34" class="t">R</text><text x="212" y="144" text-anchor="middle" class="t">r_m = √(mλR)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the lens touching the flat plate at O (left) and the concentric rings getting closer together outward (right).
cards.example: At the contact point O, thickness t = 0, so the π phase shift at the lower glass plate makes the central spot dark.
cards.bridge: From circle geometry r_m² = t(2R - t) ≈ 2Rt and the dark-ring condition 2t = mλ, the m-th dark ring has radius r_m = √(mλR).

cards.label: 02 · §15.10 Definition
cards.title: What are Newton's rings?
cards.body: Newton's rings are concentric dark and bright circular fringes formed by interference in the thin air film between a plano-convex lens of radius R and a plane glass plate.

cards.label: 03 · §15.10 Derivation
cards.title: Radii of dark rings and wavelength in Newton's rings
cards.legend: Lens of radius of curvature \(R\) on flat glass plate \(POQ\), air-film thickness \(t\) at dark ring radius \(r_m\) and diameter \(D_m = 2r_m\) (Eqs. 15.63–15.68, Fig. 15.30).

phases.name: Circle geometry
phases.why: relate ring radius r_m to film thickness t and lens radius R

phases.name: Thin air film
phases.why: neglect t compared to 2R since t ≪ R

phases.name: Dark ring radius
phases.why: substitute the dark-ring condition 2t = mλ

phases.name: Ring diameters
phases.why: write λ in terms of diameters D_{m+p} and D_m

steps.note: From the intersecting-chords relation (or right triangle \(R^2 = r_m^2 + (R - t)^2\)), \(r_m^2 = t(2R - t)\) (Eq. 15.64).

move.label: Neglect t compared to 2R for t ≪ R

steps.note: Since \(R \approx 100\text{ cm}\) and \(t \lesssim 10^{-3}\text{ cm}\), neglect \(t\) compared to \(2R\).

ask.q: Why can \(t\) be neglected inside \((2R - t)\)?
ask.why: The air film thickness \(t \lesssim 10^{-3}\text{ cm}\) is tiny compared to \(R \approx 100\text{ cm}\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(R\) to isolate \(2t\) (Eq. 15.65).
Substitute the air-film dark-ring condition \(2t = m\lambda\) (Eq. 15.63).

ask.q: For the \(m\)-th dark ring in an air film (\(n = 1\)), what is \(2t\)?
ask.why: With the \(\pi\) phase shift at the lower plate, destructive interference occurs at \(2t = m\lambda\).

steps.note: Multiply by \(R\); thus dark ring radii vary as \(\sqrt{m}\) (Eq. 15.66).

ask.q: How do the radii \(r_m\) of dark Newton's rings scale with order \(m\)?
ask.why: Since \(r_m = \sqrt{m\lambda R}\), radii grow as the square root of natural numbers \(m\).

steps.note: With diameter \(D_m = 2r_m\), \(D_{m+p}^2 - D_m^2 = 4[(m+p)\lambda R - m\lambda R] = 4p\lambda R\).
Divide both sides by \(4pR\).
Swap sides to get the wavelength formula from two ring diameters (Eq. 15.68).

ask.q: Why do we measure \(D_{m+p}^2 - D_m^2\) instead of a single diameter \(D_m^2\)?
options: Dust or imperfect contact cancels out
It makes the rings equally spaced
ask.why: Any constant gap offset at \(O\) due to dust cancels when \(r_m^2\) is subtracted from \(r_{m+p}^2\).

cards.title: Two perpendicular mirror arms acting like a tunable air film
cards.meaning: The Michelson interferometer splits a light beam at 45° toward two perpendicular mirrors M₁ and M₂, creating an equivalent air film between M₁ and the virtual image M₂'.
cards.picture: Look at beam splitter G₁, compensating plate G₂, movable mirror M₁, and virtual image M₂' separated by d = x₁ ~ x₂.
cards.example: As mirror M₁ moves toward M₂' reducing d, circular fringes collapse into the center; N collapsed fringes over distance d₀ give λ = 2d₀/N.
cards.bridge: Compensating plate G₂ equalizes the glass path in both arms so white-light fringes can be seen at d = 0.

cards.label: 04 · §15.11 Definition
cards.title: What is the Michelson interferometer?
cards.body: The Michelson interferometer uses a 45° beam splitter G₁, compensating plate G₂, and perpendicular mirrors M₁ and M₂ to form circular fringes of equal inclination with path difference 2d cos θ.

cards.label: 05 · §§15.10–15.11 Examples
cards.title: Lifting the lens & sodium doublet Δλ (Examples 15.2, 15.4)
cards.body: Raising the Newton's-rings lens or moving \(M_1\) toward \(M_2'\) causes rings to collapse to the center. For sodium (\(\lambda = 5890\text{ \AA}\)), successive disappearances every \(\Delta d = 0.289\text{ mm}\) give \(\Delta\lambda = (5890\text{ \AA})^2 / 0.578\text{ mm} \approx 6\text{ \AA}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What happens to Newton's rings when the convex lens is slowly raised above the plate?
options: The rings collapse toward the center
The rings turn into straight lines
cards.why: Increasing the central gap means a given thickness \(t = m\lambda/2\) occurs at a smaller radius, so rings collapse inward (Example 15.2).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why is a compensating plate \(G_2\) needed in a Michelson interferometer?
options: To equalize glass paths for white light
To focus circular rings without a lens
cards.why: Because refractive index varies with wavelength (dispersion), \(G_2\) ensures both beams traverse the glass plate three times for white light (§15.11).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In a Michelson interferometer, 1000 fringes collapse when \(M_1\) moves \(0.29\text{ mm}\). Find \(\lambda\) in nm.
cards.why: \(\lambda = \frac{2d_0}{N} = \frac{2 \times 0.29 \times 10^6\text{ nm}}{1000} = 580\text{ nm}\).
